articles.title: Africa’s top gold producer issues pre-closure warning to Chinese-owned mine over alleged unreported spill - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Africa’s top gold producer issues pre-closure warning to Chinese-owned mine over alleged unreported spill  Business Insider AfricaGhana's environmental authority targets Chinese-owned Cardinal and others in mining crackdown  TradingView
articles.full_text:
- Ghana’s environmental regulator has issued a pre-closure notice to Cardinal Namdini Mining.
- An official links it partly to an alleged failure to promptly report a mine-waste spill.
- The action is part of wider enforcement affecting companies from several countries.
- Namdini’s production ambitions make compliance a material operating risk for its investors.
Michael Ayamga, deputy chief executive for operations at the Environmental Protection Authority, told Reuters that the notice partly concerned a tailings pipeline disconnecting and causing a spill.
A pre-closure notice is not confirmation that the mine has shut. The report does not establish the spill’s volume or environmental damage.
Ayamga described a wider shift towards continuous enforcement. “We don’t want to be reactive but proactive,” he said. “We want to move beyond one-off visits and audits to enforcement.”
DON'T MISS THIS: Africa's top gold producer sets 2026 deadline for foreign miners to hand operations to local contractors
A new mine with substantial production ambitions
Namdini is an open-pit mine about 50 kilometres southeast of Bolgatanga, according to OR Royalties’ January disclosure. The royalty investor says Shandong operates the asset through Cardinal in partnership with a subsidiary of China Railway Construction Group.
The disclosure describes production ramping towards approximately 360,000 ounces annually over the first three years at design capacity, with an expected average of 287,000 ounces across an initial 15-year mine life. These are project expectations, not verified current annual output.
For a mine building towards its intended production rate, regulatory uncertainty matters beyond the immediate cost of corrective work.
Any interruption could affect the timing of output and cash receipts for owners and royalty holders. No shutdown or quantified financial impact has been established in this case.
DON'T MISS THIS: Africa's largest gold producer alters 20-year-old mining laws to give power back to its people
Ghana is tightening the terms of mining investment
The environmental action comes alongside changes to the way foreign miners participate in Ghana’s economy.
Reuters earlier described rules requiring surface mining work to move to Ghanaian-owned contractors and underground operations to ventures with at least 50% local ownership. Officials are also developing wage and tender benchmarks to address concerns about underbidding and worker conditions.
These measures concern different issues, but together illustrate the growing importance of regulatory compliance and local economic participation to mining investments.
The broader enforcement described by the publication includes scrutiny of other foreign operators. That does not establish identical breaches by those companies, and the Cardinal allegation should be assessed on its own evidence.

articles.title: Lesotho turns to SMEs to unlock AfCFTA trade opportunities - SABC News
articles.summary: Lesotho turns to SMEs to unlock AfCFTA trade opportunities  SABC News
articles.full_text:
Lesotho is sharpening its focus on small businesses as it looks to unlock opportunities under regional trade agreements and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). The Lesotho Trade and Industry Ministry is hosting a three-day workshop aimed at helping small businesses compete, expand and tap into Africa’s growing market.
A market of more than 1.3 billion people and a combined GDP of about 3.4 trillion US dollars, that is the opportunity presented by the African Continental Free Trade Area.
But for Lesotho, accessing that market means ensuring its small businesses are ready to compete.
“This agreement represents unprecedented opportunities for Lesotho’s businesses. Diversify their export market, integrate into value chain and upskill their operations. However, to benefit from these opportunities our SMEs need practical knowledge and skills,” says Lesotho’s Principal Secretary in the Ministry of Trade, Palesa Matobako.
The ambition goes beyond simply selling more goods. Lesotho wants increased trade to grow businesses, attract investment, build skills and create sustainable jobs for Basotho.
United Nations representative in Lesotho, Dr Jacqueline Olweya, “The success of the workshop should ultimately be reflected not only in knowledge learnt in three days of us being here but in markets, in enterprises becoming more export ready and the partnerships and synergy developed here. Products being tested against high demand.”
But opportunity means little without access. Regional and international partners are using the workshop to help businesses understand trade rules, identify competitive advantages and turn continental agreements into real commercial opportunities.
“It is not only to say you’re producing. The market is open for us as Africans, so the products should be originating from the continent, from our countries. Sell within the African continent,” says Programme Officer for Regional Trade at the SADC Secretariat, Motheba Malibeng.
Policy researcher at the Southern African Customs Union, Terence Mabaso says the focus should be on products the continent has comparative advantage on.
“You have comparative advantage in Mohair that is something that can be exploited and fully expanded on. You got advantage in Flora, having been almost at top of Africa with trees that can only grow here.”
For Lesotho, the AfCFTA is not about abandoning traditional export markets, it is about widening the net and making Basotho businesses more competitive.

articles.title: Suez Canal Authority eyes Kenya port projects in African expansion push - Urban & Transport - Egypt - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Suez Canal Authority eyes Kenya port projects in African expansion push - Urban & Transport - Egypt  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
SCA Chairman Osama Rabie held talks on Wednesday with Tunasco Chairman Abdul Wali Sharif at the authority’s headquarters in Ismailia, where the two sides discussed establishing a specialised company to carry out port and marine construction projects in Kenya.
The proposed partnership would involve the SCA through its affiliated Timsah Shipbuilding Company and would cover a range of maritime activities, including port development, marine construction, dredging, shipbuilding and training.
Rabie said the authority is seeking to expand beyond the Egyptian market and strengthen its presence in Africa by contributing to major development and infrastructure projects.
“The Suez Canal aspires to open new markets in the African hinterland and to participate seriously in development efforts,” Rabie said.
He added that the SCA is ready to transfer its technical and operational expertise to Kenya and contribute to the development of the country’s maritime infrastructure.
Rabie said the move reflects Egypt’s strategic interest in deepening economic and development partnerships with African countries, particularly in sectors where Egyptian institutions have accumulated extensive technical experience.
For his part, Sharif said Tunasco is seeking close cooperation with the Suez Canal Authority and hopes to benefit from its technical capabilities, skilled workforce and long experience in maritime industries.
He added that the proposed cooperation has received a positive response from the Kenyan government, citing the growing momentum in Egyptian-Kenyan relations over the past five years.
Sharif said meetings are expected to be held with senior Kenyan government officials in the coming period to establish a framework for cooperation and begin practical implementation steps.
 
The meeting was attended by Abdel-Hakim Zakaria, director of the SCA’s Companies Department; Ahmed Ibrahim, chairman of Timsah Shipbuilding Company; and Ehab Abdel-Fattah and Assem El-Safty, board members of the Kenyan-Egyptian company.
Tunasco is a Kenyan company involved in a range of infrastructure development projects.

articles.title: SADC transport: DR Congo calls for an African rail manufacturing industry - capmad.com
articles.summary: SADC transport: DR Congo calls for an African rail manufacturing industry  capmad.com
articles.full_text:
Kinshasa, 29 September 2026 – The representative of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at the ministerial transport forum of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) on 28 September 2026 called for the creation in Africa of a rail manufacturing industry based on a consortium integrating iron ore mining, steelmaking and rail production.
The Congolese envoy highlighted the country’s mining potential to support regional transport connectivity, stating that the authorities were ready to facilitate investments and the establishment of an industrial grouping dedicated to iron, steel and rails.
A regional rail demand that SADC still struggles to secure
SADC member states operate a railway network of around 40,000 kilometres, placing rail at the centre of strategies to ease congestion on the region’s main road and port corridors. Regional assessments stress that underinvestment in rail has shifted a significant share of so-called rail-friendly freight onto road, accelerating the deterioration of key highways.
Kinshasa had already, through the Ministry of Transport, Channels of Communication and Disenclavement, issued an international call for expressions of interest referenced AMI n°006/2025 – VPM/MTVCD/RAIL to set up a national rail manufacturing plant. The scheme aims to turn the DRC into a regional production hub serving not only its own network, but also railway projects in Central and Southern Africa.
DR Congo seeks to align industrial policy with rail projects
Congolese authorities draw attention to a diversified mining base – including cobalt, copper, tin, nickel-chromium, gold and diamonds – and single out steel and transport equipment value chains as diversification levers to capture more added value within the country.
In parallel, the early-September 2026 resumption of urban train services between Kinshasa’s Central Station and N’Djili international airport, after track works carried out by the Office national des transports, illustrates the renewed focus on rail in the capital’s mobility policy. Recent inspections of sites earmarked for future industrial units in Kinshasa by the Ministry of Entrepreneurship and SME Development are part of this broader agenda to relocalise industrial production.
Several strategic corridors in the region – from the Zambian and Congolese Copperbelt to ports in South Africa and Mozambique – are undergoing rail modernisation programmes to reduce logistics costs and improve freight reliability. International assessments also note that the recovery of legacy Congolese operators such as Société nationale des chemins de fer du Congo will be key to the country’s full integration into these corridors.
Towards a timetable for the African rail consortium
The call for expressions of interest referenced AMI n°006/2025 – VPM/MTVCD/RAIL provides for the shortlisting of technical, industrial and financial partners responsible for designing, financing, building, equipping and operating the national rail manufacturing plant. At the same time, the 2026 procurement plan of the Ministry of Transport already frames several tenders relating to railway infrastructure, offering an initial pipeline of projects that a future local production capacity could service.
Discussions launched within SADC on the back of this Congolese call for an African consortium are now expected to continue in the technical working groups in charge of implementing regional rail programmes.
